paragraphs: This paper learns document representations from text without requiring labels. Its central task is to predict the probability of another word given words already observed in the document. By learning these predictions, the model also learns a representation that summarizes information about the document’s content.

The architecture takes inspiration from the recursive inference equations of Replicated Softmax, a model of word counts. The authors use those equations to motivate a neural network with conditional word predictions. This construction also permits a computational shortcut: instead of evaluating a flat distribution across the vocabulary, the model assigns probabilities through paths in a binary tree of words.

That tree changes how training cost depends on vocabulary size, making this dependence logarithmic rather than linear as in Replicated Softmax. The reported experiments find the resulting model competitive both at modeling documents probabilistically and at learning document representations. The contribution therefore connects useful text representations with a more favorable vocabulary-dependent training cost.
neurips-2012-a-neural-autoregressive-top.tldr: A neural document model predicts words through a binary tree, reducing vocabulary-dependent training cost while learning competitive document representations.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to make the relationships among many measured variables easier to interpret. Factor analysis can summarize their covariance structure, describing how variables vary together, but its resulting representation can be difficult to understand. The authors pursue a more explicit summary: divide the observed variables into separate groups whose members are highly correlated.

The objects being clustered are the variables themselves. The desired result is a disjoint partition, so each variable belongs to one group. This gives the representation a direct interpretation: a group collects measurements that tend to vary together. The proposed approach frames this grouping problem using Bayesian nonparametric modeling, providing a probabilistic alternative to the heuristic methods discussed in the paper.

The authors report advantages over those heuristic approaches. The stated contribution is therefore both a modeling choice and an interpretability goal: use a Bayesian framework to seek clearly separated groups of related variables. It offers another way to summarize high-dimensional covariance when an explicit grouping is the desired output.
neurips-2012-a-nonparametric-variable-cl.tldr: A Bayesian nonparametric model groups correlated variables into disjoint clusters to make high-dimensional covariance structure easier to interpret.

paragraphs: Robust regression aims to fit relationships without allowing unusual observations to dominate the answer. The paper identifies a difficult tradeoff in existing formulations: they can be computationally intractable, or they can respond without bound to even one leverage point. That makes computational feasibility and resistance to influential observations joint concerns.

The authors introduce Variational M-estimation, a general formulation that brings several robust regression methods into a common framework. Its practical purpose is to permit a tractable approximation strategy. From this formulation, they develop an estimator with polynomial-time computation and certain guarantees concerning robustness and consistency. The claim concerns this estimator and its stated guarantees, rather than exact efficient solutions to every robust regression problem.

Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed estimation approach relative to standard methods. Together, the theoretical and experimental contributions show a route toward balancing manageable computation with statistically meaningful protection against problematic observations. The unifying formulation matters because it connects that route to a broader family of robust regression approaches.
neurips-2012-a-polynomial-time-form-of-r.tldr: Variational M-estimation supports a polynomial-time robust regression estimator with qualified robustness and consistency guarantees.

paragraphs: The paper studies functions whose inputs have many coordinates but whose values depend on only a few linear combinations of them. More specifically, the function is a sum of component functions, each acting on one such combination. The goal is to learn this structure by choosing input locations and observing the function’s values there.

The authors propose a randomized active sampling method and analyze it using tools from low-rank matrix recovery. Their setting assumes inputs lie in a Euclidean ball, the lower-dimensional function is twice continuously differentiable almost everywhere, and the projection matrix has full row rank. Its number of rows is much smaller than the input dimension, expressing the assumed low-dimensional structure.

Under the studied setting, the method provides uniform approximation guarantees and bounds on the number of evaluations required. The paper also characterizes sensitivity to noise. Empirical results support the predicted dependence of sample requirements on the high input dimension, connecting the theoretical analysis to observed scaling behavior.
neurips-2012-active-learning-of-multi-in.tldr: A randomized active sampling method learns functions of a few linear projections with approximation, sample-complexity, and noise-robustness analysis.

paragraphs: This paper develops an online method for updating the smoothing functions in an additive model as observations arrive. The objective is to follow changing relationships over time, a useful requirement for electricity demand forecasting. The approach combines a linear representation of the additive model with a Recursive Least Squares filter.

The filter discounts older observations exponentially through a forgetting factor, giving recent data greater influence. The authors then make this factor adaptive: it changes using the gradient of prediction errors computed before updating the model. This adds a mechanism for adjusting how strongly past observations influence current learning. The paper also uses Lyapunov stability theory to analyze upper bounds on the learning rate.

The method is evaluated using five years of electricity load observations from EDF. In that application, the authors report better model tracking and prediction accuracy than the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support adaptive forgetting as a practical way to keep an additive forecasting model responsive to changing data.
neurips-2012-adaptive-learning-of-smooth.tldr: An online additive-model learner adapts its forgetting rate to track changing electricity demand and improve forecasting in the reported evaluation.

paragraphs: This paper considers optimization problems that change with a single parameter. Instead of seeking a solution at just one parameter value, it studies how to represent the solution path as that parameter varies. The defining condition is that the optimization problem depends concavely on the parameter, which specifies the class covered by the results.

For any positive accuracy target epsilon, the authors show that a set of size proportional to one over the square root of epsilon can approximate the path. They also prove a matching lower bound up to a constant factor. This means the dependence on accuracy cannot generally be improved across the studied class merely by finding a different approximation strategy.

The paper supplies an algorithm that achieves this path size by consulting a step-size oracle. It also implements that oracle for soft-margin support vector machines and a parameterized semidefinite program for matrix completion. These constructions connect the abstract approximation result to concrete optimization problems with adjustable parameters.
neurips-2012-approximating-concavely-par.tldr: For concavely parameterized optimization problems, the paper proves tight bounds on approximate solution-path size and gives an oracle-based construction.

paragraphs: This paper addresses a weakness of clustering with nonnegative matrix factorization: directly fitting pairwise similarities can emphasize only immediate relationships between samples. For data arranged along curved manifolds, those local comparisons may fail to capture relationships that become visible through connections among multiple samples. The authors seek to bring those farther relationships into the clustering objective.

Their method uses a random walk to smooth the similarity matrix before factorizing it. The resulting target incorporates relationships beyond immediate sample pairs. They also introduce a regularization term intended to improve on spectral clustering. A multiplicative Majorization-Minimization algorithm optimizes the resulting objective, with an implementation designed to make learning the factor matrix scalable.

Experiments across real-world datasets show strong cluster purity, meaning the discovered groups align well with the evaluated class groupings. The reported evidence supports combining graph-based smoothing with factorization. The central contribution is the change in what the factorization tries to represent: similarities enriched by paths through the data graph.
neurips-2012-clustering-by-nonnegative-m.tldr: Random-walk smoothing lets nonnegative matrix factorization use farther relationships between samples, with strong reported clustering purity.

paragraphs: The paper learns preferences from comparisons supplied by multiple users, where each observation indicates a preference between two alternatives. It uses Gaussian processes to model these judgments while sharing information across users. The aim is to capture both individual preferences and common patterns in user behavior.

A preference kernel simplifies inference and connects supervised learning from comparisons with unsupervised dimensionality reduction across users. This lets the model exploit shared structure rather than treating every user’s observations in isolation. When descriptions or other features of users are available, the framework can incorporate them as well. Approximate inference combines expectation propagation with variational Bayes.

The authors also develop an efficient active learning strategy for selecting which preference comparisons to ask about. Thus, the framework addresses both learning from existing judgments and choosing additional queries. Evaluation on real-world data finds favorable performance against state-of-the-art multi-user preference-learning algorithms, supporting the usefulness of collaborative structure in the tested preference tasks.
neurips-2012-collaborative-gaussian-proc.tldr: A collaborative Gaussian-process model learns pairwise preferences by sharing structure across users and actively selecting further comparisons.

paragraphs: This paper asks how neural circuits might carry out probabilistic reasoning beyond relatively simple computations. Probabilistic population codes represent probability distributions through population activity, but earlier applications emphasized tasks such as combining cues. The authors show how a more general approximate inference procedure, Variational Bayesian Expectation Maximization, can be implemented within a linear population-code framework.

Their example is separating a mixture of spikes into its hidden causes. They establish a formal correspondence between this problem and the document topic model Latent Dirichlet Allocation. Using that correspondence, they construct a neural network that performs approximate inference and learning for the topic model through a linear probabilistic population code.

The network critically uses divisive normalization and super-linear facilitation, two nonlinear operations observed widely in neural circuits. The paper also shows online learning through a variation of Hebb’s rule and describes an extension for correlated causes that change over time. The contribution is a concrete computational account of how this coding framework could support more complex inference.
neurips-2012-complex-inference-in-neural.tldr: A neural implementation of topic-model inference extends probabilistic population coding to separating complex spike mixtures into latent causes.

paragraphs: This paper studies online multiclass learning using the confusion matrix as the performance measure. A confusion matrix records which classes are mistaken for which others, preserving information about the pattern of errors. The authors describe their work as the first analysis of this setting to their knowledge, retaining that qualification on the novelty claim.

The theoretical development uses concentration inequalities for matrices, particularly matrix martingales. These tools support generalization bounds for online learning algorithms when performance is described through a matrix. The analysis therefore addresses how performance on the observed sequence relates to broader predictive behavior while keeping the structure of class confusions in view.

The theory also motivates a learning procedure called COnfusion Passive-Aggressive, or COPA. Its update equations have analytic solutions, so implementing those updates does not require a general optimization package. The contribution connects a structured view of prediction errors with both generalization analysis and a concrete online algorithm designed around that view.
neurips-2012-confusion-based-online-lear.tldr: Confusion-matrix generalization bounds motivate COPA, an online multiclass learner whose updates can be computed analytically.

paragraphs: The paper introduces decision forests that use intermediate predictions as contextual information during object detection. Each sample can access classification and regression information produced within the prediction process. This capability is available during both training and inference, allowing later decisions to take account of predictions already being formed.

The authors use this information to define context-dependent decision criteria that refine the prediction process. They also propose a new splitting criterion and a priority-based procedure for constructing trees. Together, these changes allow more accurate selection of regression modes, which improves the context available to the forest. Intermediate predictions consequently become information that the model can use in further decisions.

Experiments on pedestrian detection using the TUD dataset show improved results relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. The evidence supports the proposed use of evolving prediction information in that detection setting. The broader methodological contribution is a decision-forest framework in which context participates directly in the tree-based prediction process.
neurips-2012-context-sensitive-decision-.tldr: Context-sensitive decision forests reuse intermediate predictions to refine object detection, improving reported pedestrian-detection results.

paragraphs: Finding the most probable assignment in a graphical model is generally difficult, so practitioners often solve a linear programming relaxation. Message-passing algorithms can update coordinates of the relaxation’s dual problem, but these updates do not generally guarantee convergence to a global optimum. Smoothing the relaxation offers a way to address this difficulty.

The paper analyzes how quickly coordinate minimization converges on the smoothed dual. It derives convergence rates for both the dual formulation used by the updates and the primal formulation of the optimization problem. This matters because progress in the internal optimization representation must ultimately translate into useful solutions to the problem being solved.

The authors also provide a simple conversion from dual iterates to feasible primal solutions, with a guaranteed convergence rate. Experiments support the theoretical claims and show competitive performance against approaches that obtain global optima. These conclusions concern solving the relaxation framework; they do not establish that every resulting solution exactly solves the original discrete assignment problem.
neurips-2012-convergence-rate-analysis-o.tldr: The paper establishes convergence rates and feasible-solution recovery for coordinate methods applied to smoothed MAP linear-programming relaxations.

paragraphs: This paper studies probabilistic learning when observations are spread across a sensor network and some measurements are unavailable. Centralized vision algorithms assume access to all observed data, but physical or computational constraints can make distributed processing desirable. The authors also identify missing data as a difficulty for existing distributed approaches based primarily on algebraic factorization.

Their contribution is a distributed approach to estimating generative probabilistic models. In particular, they show how probabilistic principal component analysis and its missing-data version can be learned with observations distributed across sensors. This extends models usually learned centrally to a setting where the data reside at different network locations.

The application is distributed affine structure from motion, which estimates structure and motion from visual observations. Experiments suggest that the learned models achieve accuracy comparable to traditional centralized factorization methods while handling challenging missing or noisy measurements. The findings support distributed probabilistic modeling as a practical option for camera networks facing incomplete observations.
neurips-2012-distributed-probabilistic-l.tldr: Distributed probabilistic learning extends PCA-based camera-network models to missing observations, with accuracy reported to rival centralized factorization.

paragraphs: Neural spike counts can vary more than a Poisson model allows. This paper uses the negative-binomial distribution to model that extra variability and develops a framework for fully Bayesian inference. The goal is to characterize neural responses while supporting statistical models of both measured influences and hidden population structure.

The computational step is data augmentation using a latent-variable representation involving a Polya-gamma mixture of normal distributions. With the added variables, the posterior has a conditionally Gaussian representation. This does not say the entire posterior is Gaussian; it provides a tractable conditional structure from which the authors construct efficient EM and Gibbs sampling algorithms for regression and dynamic factor models.

On neural recordings from primate retina, the model substantially outperforms Poisson regression on held-out observations. It also reveals latent structure associated with correlations among simultaneously recorded spike counts. These results support combining a model of greater-than-Poisson variability with inference machinery that makes richer neural response models computationally accessible.
neurips-2012-fully-bayesian-inference-fo.tldr: Latent-variable augmentation enables Bayesian negative-binomial neural models that improve held-out prediction and reveal correlated spike-count structure.

paragraphs: This paper proposes an image representation that captures spatial relationships among local visual features. It models their distribution with a Gaussian Markov Random Field, then uses the model’s parameters to describe the image. The resulting Graphical Gaussian Vector offers an alternative to representations built around codebooks or direct matching of local features.

The authors use information geometry to select suitable parameters and a metric for the probabilistic model. They then incorporate that metric into the parameter-based feature representation. This produces a vector that can be used directly by scalable linear classifiers, connecting a structured model of local relationships to a comparatively simple classification stage.

The reported evaluations show better performance than the compared state-of-the-art methods on standard object-recognition datasets and comparable performance on a scene dataset. The method computes local autocorrelations of features, which the authors identify as supporting both efficiency and classification accuracy. The findings suggest that spatial statistical relationships can provide useful image information without requiring a costly final classifier.
neurips-2012-graphical-gaussian-vector-f.tldr: Graphical Gaussian Vectors encode spatial feature relationships in an image vector suitable for efficient linear classification.

paragraphs: This paper develops a probabilistic model of sound with two levels of spiking representation. The first level describes an acoustic signal through a sparse collection of kernels at different frequencies, each placed precisely in time. This gives the model a representation of when particular acoustic components occur.

The second level captures broader patterns in the timing and frequencies of those first-level spikes. Recurrent interactions within the first level capture finer statistical regularities. The division assigns structure at different scales to different parts of the model: higher-level spikes describe coarser organization, while interactions among lower-level elements account for more detailed relationships.

When fitted to speech, the model represents features including harmonic stacks, frequency sweeps, and frequency modulations that can combine into more complex acoustic events. It can also synthesize sounds from the higher-level representation. On a denoising task, it significantly improves over wavelet thresholding techniques, supporting the practical value of the learned multiscale acoustic structure in the reported evaluation.
neurips-2012-hierarchical-spike-coding-o.tldr: A two-level probabilistic spike model captures acoustic structure at multiple scales and improves sound denoising over wavelet thresholding.

paragraphs: The paper seeks recurring brain-activity patterns in fMRI recordings without observing the associated mental states directly. This requires comparing spatial activity patterns across time while managing high dimensionality and measurement artifacts. The authors propose a compact feature space that incorporates the connectivity of the network on which activity is measured.

The representation comes from a spherical relaxation of transportation distance. Transportation distance compares two patterns through the cost of moving activity mass over the network to transform one into the other. Its approximation provides a way to compare and cluster network states while respecting network connections, with computational efficiency and relative resistance to structured and random noise.

Theoretical and empirical assessments support the approximation’s accuracy and efficiency, particularly for large problems. The presented application identifies distinct activity patterns in fMRI. The authors also describe broader applicability to recurring-pattern discovery and outlier detection on other networks, including sensor, control, and social networks; these are proposed uses of the same network-aware representation.
neurips-2012-identification-of-recurrent.tldr: A compact approximation to network transportation distance enables efficient, relatively noise-robust discovery of recurring fMRI activity patterns.

paragraphs: This paper extends latent support vector machines to use kernel methods. Latent SVMs have been useful in computer vision, but the authors identify their reliance on linear models as a limitation. Their motivation is that nonlinear kernel models often perform better on visual tasks where a linear model is suboptimal.

The proposed Kernel Latent SVM combines latent SVM modeling with the flexibility supplied by kernels. The authors also develop an iterative procedure for learning its parameters. This makes the contribution both a modeling framework and a training approach: the paper explains how to incorporate nonlinear modeling into the latent-SVM setting and how to fit the resulting model.

The framework is evaluated on three visual-recognition applications, with results demonstrating its effectiveness. The authors present the formulation as general enough for a broad range of computer-vision and machine-learning applications. The stated evidence establishes usefulness in the evaluated tasks, while the general formulation motivates potential use beyond those particular demonstrations.
neurips-2012-kernel-latent-svm-for-visua.tldr: Kernel Latent SVM combines latent-variable SVM modeling with nonlinear kernels and demonstrates effectiveness on three visual-recognition applications.

paragraphs: This paper learns a lower-dimensional representation in which distances reflect known labels. It finds linear projections that bring similarly labeled inputs closer together and push differently labeled inputs farther apart. The same construction therefore supports supervised dimensionality reduction and learning a distance metric suited to the labeled data.

The model introduces continuous hidden variables that position pairs of examples in a lower-dimensional space. Unlike classical factor analysis, the posterior distribution over these variables is not always multivariate Gaussian. Nevertheless, the authors show that inference remains fully tractable and derive an Expectation-Maximization algorithm for estimating the model’s parameters.

The appealing computational feature is the metric update: each EM iteration re-estimates the distance metric by solving an unconstrained least-squares problem. This makes the repeated fitting step simple despite the more unusual posterior structure. Comparisons with other distance-learning approaches and the reported experiments show that these simple updates are highly effective, supporting the model’s combination of probabilistic structure and straightforward optimization.
neurips-2012-latent-coincidence-analysis.tldr: A latent-variable model learns label-sensitive distances through tractable EM inference and simple unconstrained least-squares metric updates.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate a manifold from randomly sampled points. It examines two ways of building an approximation from simpler pieces: k-means produces a piecewise constant representation, while k-flats produces a piecewise linear one. The question is how well these representations reconstruct the underlying manifold.

The authors extend the theory of k-means reconstruction on manifolds and establish reconstruction bounds for k-flats. The latter addresses a higher-order approximation: local linear pieces can represent structure differently from isolated representative points. The analysis gives mathematical bounds for these estimators, providing a basis for assessing reconstruction quality beyond their use as computational procedures.

The paper distinguishes the novelty of its two contributions. Its k-means results are new but use some established analytical tools. For k-flats, it reports both new reconstruction results, where none were previously known, and new mathematical techniques. The contribution is therefore principally theoretical, expanding what can be established about manifold approximation from random samples.
neurips-2012-learning-manifolds-with-k-m.tldr: The paper establishes new manifold-reconstruction bounds for k-means and k-flats, including new analytical tools for piecewise linear approximation.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a Deep Boltzmann Machine that learns a joint generative model of multiple data types. Its experiments focus on images paired with text. By modeling their joint probability distribution, the system learns representations that can draw on relationships between visual and textual information.

The model can also form a representation when some modalities are absent by sampling from conditional distributions. This supports retrieval queries containing one modality or multiple modalities. The authors find the learned representations useful for classification and information retrieval, interpreting that usefulness as evidence that they capture some notion of semantic similarity.

Experiments show that the model learns a useful joint image-and-text distribution and supports retrieval with both unimodal and multimodal queries. The authors also report significant gains over SVMs and LDA on discriminative tasks and over compared deep learning methods, including autoencoders and deep belief networks. These findings support joint generative learning as a way to obtain representations useful across the evaluated prediction and retrieval settings.
neurips-2012-multimodal-learning-with-de.tldr: A multimodal Deep Boltzmann Machine learns joint image-text representations that support missing modalities, classification, and information retrieval.

paragraphs: This paper develops optimization methods for estimating a sparse inverse covariance matrix. The methods use second-order information about the objective to choose updates. A central computational concern is how to benefit from this curvature information without explicitly storing the full Hessian matrix.

The first approach, Newton-LASSO, constructs a piecewise quadratic approximation at each iteration and solves the resulting subproblem with FISTA. The second, Orthant-Based Newton, first selects a face corresponding to a pattern of signs and zeros, then uses conjugate gradients to minimize a smooth quadratic approximation there. Both exploit Hessian structure when computing search directions.

The authors also show that quasi-Newton approaches are effective and describe a limited-memory BFGS version of the orthant-based method. Numerical results suggest that the proposed techniques have useful practical properties, and the paper compares them with the method in QUIC. The evidence supports them as additional tools for this estimation problem without claiming that one approach uniformly dominates the others.
neurips-2012-newton-like-methods-for-spa.tldr: Newton and quasi-Newton methods exploit curvature efficiently to solve sparse inverse covariance estimation without storing the full Hessian.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to group data points into low-dimensional subspaces when outliers are present. It formulates the task through density estimation and an associated generative model. This provides a probabilistic basis for estimating the underlying low-dimensional structure while addressing observations that do not fit it.

Starting from this model, the authors develop an iterative Expectation-Maximization algorithm and derive its global solution. They then introduce two variational Bayesian methods that can select dimensionality automatically. One alternates optimization over the unknown quantities; the other uses results from variational Bayesian matrix factorization to obtain fast and effective estimation.

Both Bayesian methods are extended to account for sparse outliers and can also handle missing values. These capabilities connect dimensionality selection, robustness, and incomplete observations within the proposed framework. Experiments suggest that the methods work very effectively for clustering and identifying outliers. The global-solution result belongs to the initial model development and should not be read as a blanket guarantee for every Bayesian extension.
neurips-2012-probabilistic-low-rank-subs.tldr: A probabilistic subspace-clustering framework supports automatic dimensionality selection, sparse outliers, and missing observations.

paragraphs: This paper examines a recurring difficulty in statistical modeling: greater flexibility and robustness can make an estimation problem harder to compute. Its setting is high-dimensional nonparanormal graph estimation, a semiparametric graphical-model problem. The aim is to estimate the graph efficiently while retaining theoretical control over the statistical procedure.

The authors propose smooth-projected neighborhood pursuit and provide new computational and theoretical analysis. Smoothing is central to their treatment of the optimization problem. The resulting framework allows them to study computational efficiency and statistical error together, making the cost of obtaining an estimate part of the analysis of its quality.

The paper reports theoretical guarantees for the proposed method and experiments using text and stock datasets. Its contribution is both an estimation procedure and a perspective on the tradeoff between computation and statistical accuracy. The application results illustrate the method in two data settings, while the smoothing framework provides the basis for analyzing how numerical choices interact with estimation error.
neurips-2012-smooth-projected-neighborho.tldr: Smooth-projected neighborhood pursuit estimates nonparanormal graphs while analyzing the tradeoff between computational efficiency and statistical error.

paragraphs: This paper introduces the transelliptical distribution family for robust estimation of high-dimensional graphical models. The construction extends elliptical distributions by allowing separate univariate transformations of the variables. It follows the same broad idea by which nonparanormal models extend normal distributions, but starts from a broader underlying family.

The authors propose a regularized estimator based on ranks rather than a fully specified parametric distribution. Their theoretical result is that it achieves parametric convergence rates for both recovering the graph and estimating model parameters. These are distinct goals: identifying the graph’s structure and accurately estimating the quantities that describe the model.

Matching those rates suggests that the added robustness and modeling flexibility come with almost no loss of statistical efficiency. That is a conclusion about convergence rates, not a claim that all finite-sample behavior is identical. The paper also discusses connections to transelliptical component analysis, placing graph estimation alongside another use of the same distribution family.
neurips-2012-transelliptical-graphical-m.tldr: Rank-based estimation for transelliptical graphical models achieves parametric convergence rates while allowing greater distributional flexibility and robustness.
